title: Portfolio Listings
text:
What Is a Listing?
A listing is a Quarto feature that automatically builds a page of links, like a blog index or a project portfolio, from a set of items. Instead of hand-coding a card for every project, I describe each project once, and Quarto generates the cards, the sorting, the search box, and the category filters for me.






NoteWhy listings are useful for a portfolio




Consistent: every project gets the same layout.
Easy to update: adding a project is one new entry, not new HTML.
Interactive: visitors can search, sort, and filter by topic.

title: Portfolio Listings
section: Two Ways to Fill a Listing
text:
Two Ways to Fill a Listing

From a YAML file (what I used)From Quarto documents


All my projects live in one file, projects.yml. Each item has a title, description, link, image, date, and categories:
- title: "CEP Dashboard: Paid vs. Organic Search"
  description: "A Quarto dashboard comparing paid and organic search..."
  path: cep-dashboard.qmd
  image: images/projects/cep-dashboard.svg
  date: "2026-10-22"
  categories: [Dashboard, GA4, R]
This works best for a portfolio, because many of my projects live on other pages or in other repositories.


For a blog, each post is its own .qmd file inside a folder, and the listing reads the title, date, and categories from each post’s YAML header:
listing:
  contents: posts
  sort: "date desc"
  type: default
  categories: true
New posts appear automatically the next time the site renders.

title: CEP Dashboard
text:
For my MSDM Culminating Experience Project (CEP), my team is consulting for the CPP Farm Store at Kellogg Ranch. Each team member leads one analytics objective, and mine focuses on the store’s websites:






NoteMy Analytics Objective (AO4)



Analyze GA4 conversion path data to evaluate whether Google Shopping Ads would improve traffic-to-purchase conversion.


The store’s own GA4 data is not connected yet, so this dashboard uses Google’s public GA4 sample e-commerce dataset (Google Merchandise Store). It has the exact same structure as a real GA4 export, so the same code will run on Farm Store data later.1

title: CEP Dashboard
text:
How the Dashboard Is Built
The dashboard is a single Quarto file with format: dashboard. Its headings become the layout, and each code chunk becomes a card.

PagesRows and CardsValue BoxesTheme


Each level-one heading (#) is a page in the dashboard’s navigation bar:



Table 1: Dashboard pages









Page
What it shows




Overview
Value boxes with key numbers, conversion by channel, and the purchase funnel


Paid vs. Organic
A chi-square test comparing paid and organic search, with takeaways for the Farm Store


Data
The full table of users and funnel steps by channel, plus a note on the source









## Row {height="22%"} creates a row and sets its height.
### Conversion {width="45%"} creates a column inside a row and sets its width.
Every chunk with #| title: becomes a titled card, and ::: {.card title="..."} wraps text in a card.



#| content: valuebox
#| title: "Paid search conversion"
list(icon = "megaphone", color = "#C98A9B", value = percent(cr_cpc, 0.01))
Value boxes use Bootstrap icons and my brand colors, so the numbers stand out at a glance.


The dashboard uses the same theme as this website, cosmo layered with my own styles/theme.scss, and the plots use a matching color palette. That keeps the dashboard and the site looking like one brand.

title: CEP Dashboard
text:
Key Findings

Organic search brings the most visitors of any channel.
Paid search converts lower than organic search, and the difference is statistically significant.
Across every channel, only about 1 in 5 visitors views a product, and fewer than 1 in 4 product viewers add to cart, so product discovery and product pages are worth improving before buying more traffic.







TipRecommendation for the Farm Store



Strengthen organic SEO first, set a GA4 baseline, and then test Google Shopping Ads in a short, tracked campaign before committing a larger budget.

title: CEP Dashboard
text:
Footnotes


The data was pulled from bigquery-public-data.ga4_obfuscated_sample_ecommerce in Google BigQuery with SQL, rolled up to one row per traffic channel, and saved as a CSV in this site’s data folder.↩︎

title: Styling with CSS and SCSS
text:
Quarto gives every website a clean default look, but a portfolio should feel like you. With CSS and SCSS, I can control colors, fonts, spacing, and components across every page from one or two files, instead of formatting each page by hand. That keeps my personal brand consistent, which matters a lot in beauty and fashion marketing, where visual identity is everything.






NoteThe short version




HTML is the structure of a page (headings, paragraphs, images).
CSS is the style rules that decide how that structure looks.
SCSS (Sass) is CSS with superpowers: variables, nesting, and reusable values.

NoteThe short version

CSS is the style rules that decide how that structure looks.
SCSS (Sass) is CSS with superpowers: variables, nesting, and reusable values.

title: Styling with CSS and SCSS
Styling with CSS and SCSS
Styling with CSS and SCSS
text:
How Quarto Uses SCSS
A Quarto SCSS theme file has two special sections:



Table 2: The two sections of a Quarto SCSS file










Section
What goes in it
Example from my site




/*-- scss:defaults --*/
Variables, including Bootstrap and Quarto ones
$body-bg: $cream;


/*-- scss:rules --*/
Regular CSS rules that use those variables
.navbar .nav-link { ... }






I layer my theme on top of the Bootswatch cosmo theme in _quarto.yml, so I only override what I want to change:
format:
  html:
    theme:
      - cosmo
      - styles/theme.scss
    css: styles/extras.css






TipOrder matters



Later themes override earlier ones. Because theme.scss comes after cosmo, my colors and fonts win. The extra extras.css file loads last and holds layout pieces like the hero and timeline.

title: Styling with CSS and SCSS
text:
My Design Choices

Color Palette
I chose a soft, editorial palette inspired by beauty brand websites: deep burgundy for confidence, blush and sky blue for softness, and warm cream instead of plain white.






Burgundy $burgundy#6B2737







Plum $plum#8A4B5E







Blush $blush#F3D9DC







Sky $sky#CFE3F1







Cream $cream#FBF7F1







Ink $ink#2B2326





Fonts
I load three Google Fonts with one @import line in the SCSS defaults:

Playfair Display for headings: an elegant, high-contrast serif with a fashion-magazine feel.
Pinyon Script for small accents, like the “Hi, I’m” on my home page.
Inter for body text: clean and easy to read at any size.



Accessibility
Pretty only works if people can read it. I kept dark ink text on a light cream background for strong contrast, used the script font only for short decorative words, and never rely on color alone to carry meaning.1

title: Julieta Diaz
text:
About Me
I bring together three things I care about: psychology, marketing, and data. My undergraduate training in psychology taught me why consumers make the choices they do, and the MSDM program is giving me the analytics and technical skills to measure and act on those choices.
Outside the classroom, I work in public sector administration, where I manage contract documentation and communication across departments, and I run Juke Vintage, my own secondhand and vintage clothing resale shop. Running a small fashion business has given me hands-on experience with product photography, listings, pricing, and what makes a shopper click “buy.”

title: Julieta Diaz
text:
Career Aspirations

I want to transition into the beauty industry, where I can combine my passion for marketing, data analytics, and consumer behavior to develop innovative digital marketing strategies.

Ultimately, I hope to grow into a leadership role where I can use data-driven insights and creativity to influence decisions and help brands connect with their consumers.
